relationship: God asked to deal mercifully with communal sins
rationale: Psalm 64 acknowledges overpowering lawless deeds and says God will make atonement for impieties. Psalm 78 asks the saving God to be propitious toward the community's sins. The comparison concerns divine action toward confessed communal wrongdoing.

relationship: Divine care for rain-fed land throughout the year
rationale: The psalm blesses the year's crown of divine kindness and rich plains. Deuteronomy describes hills and plains drinking heaven's rain under God's care from the year's beginning to its end. Both connect annual divine care with the land's fertility.

relationship: Payment of vows within God's house
rationale: The speaker enters God's house and pays vows. Psalm 115 likewise locates paying vows to the Lord in the house's courts before the people. The vow and sanctuary setting are both explicit.

relationship: Wrongdoing and the refusal of prayer
rationale: The psalm places regard for injustice in the heart under the condition that the Lord not hear. Isaiah refuses multiplied supplication from blood-filled hands and commands removal of evil and pursuit of justice. The parallel preserves the psalm's condition rather than declaring it a confession of actual injustice.

relationship: Divine salvation announced as good news
rationale: Psalm 67 says the Lord will give an utterance to those announcing good news. Isaiah describes the good-news messenger and God's making salvation heard. The comparison is the divinely supplied proclamation, without importing a gender or number of messengers absent from the psalm's wording.

relationship: God chooses a dwelling and remains there
rationale: Psalm 67 speaks of the mountain in which God pleased to dwell and His continuing residence. Psalm 131 explicitly says God chose Zion for His dwelling and rest. The parallel is divine choice and enduring dwelling; it does not supply an unnamed mountain's identity merely from the shared theme.

relationship: Women with tambourines accompany victory praise
rationale: The psalm's musicians include young women beating tambourines. Exodus describes Miriam and women with timbrels and dances, leading praise after the sea deliverance. This is a specific musical comparison, not an identification of the psalm's procession with Miriam's occasion.

relationship: Egypt and Ethiopia brought into acknowledgment of Israel's God
rationale: Psalm 67 names Egyptian envoys and Ethiopia hastening its hand toward God. Isaiah brings Egypt's labor and Ethiopians' trade into a scene of people in bonds acknowledging Israel's God. The named nations and divine acknowledgment correspond, while the differing modes of approach remain distinct.

relationship: Adversaries add affliction beyond divine displeasure
rationale: Psalm 68 accuses opponents of persecuting the one God struck and adding pain to His wounded. Zechariah condemns nations that joined in attack to bring evils when God was a little angry. Both distinguish God's displeasure from adversaries' additional assault.

relationship: Earth, watery depths and creeping creatures summoned to praise
rationale: Psalm 68 calls the sea and all creeping things in it, along with heaven and earth, to praise. Psalm 148 calls the earth, deeps and creeping things into its creation-wide praise. The sea/deeps and creature groups form the particular comparison.

relationship: God asked not to put His help far away
rationale: Both combine a request against divine distance with a call to attend to help or support. The paired distance-and-attending clauses supply the correspondence.

Psalm 70 asks that slanderers and evil-seekers wrap themselves in shame and confusion. Psalm 108 asks that slanderers wear humiliation and wrap shame like a double cloak. The clothing image and the slanderers' role correspond.

relationship: Divine mighty acts announced to the coming generation
rationale: Psalm 70 asks for continued support until God's power and righteousness are announced to the coming generation. Psalm 77 describes transmission of His mighty acts to children yet to be born so they will hope in Him. The intergenerational purpose is explicit in both.

relationship: The whole earth filled with the Lord's glory
rationale: Psalm 71 wishes the whole earth filled with divine glory. Numbers states in the Lord's oath that His glory shall fill all the earth. The same worldwide filling by glory occurs in a doxology and in divine speech.
